issues.legal_issue: The discretion to assess the income of an association collectively or its members individually does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality when it is guided by the tax authority’s quasi-judicial duties and subject to appeal.
material_facts: The tax authority could assess income either in the hands of an association of persons or in the hands of its members individually.
The assessment procedure was the same under either approach, and the authority’s decision was appealable to higher tax authorities.
The tax authority was required to administer the tax law in the public revenue’s interests, prevent evasion or escape from tax, and avoid taxing the same income more than once.
issues.conclusion: The statutory discretion to select the association or its members for assessment was not arbitrary or unguided and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a statutory discretion where the statute’s scheme, purpose, and surrounding circumstances provide adequate guidance for its exercise. The Court applied Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar, Jyoti Pershad v. The Administrator for the Union Territory of Delhi, and Commissioner of Income-tax v. Kanpur Coal Syndicate. It distinguished Suraj Mall Mohta & Co. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri because that case involved a more drastic alternative procedure that deprived assessees of valuable review rights. The Court also considered the scheme of section 3 and the legislative history of section 23A of the Income-tax Act, 1922, including its repeal, and held that the repeal did not turn the authority’s discretion into arbitrary power.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment_discretion and (quasi_judicial_assessment or appellate_review) and public_revenue_duty and (evasion_risk or double_taxation_risk)

predicates.income_tax_assessment_discretion: The proceeding concerns a tax authority choosing whether to assess income collectively in the hands of an association or separately in the hands of its members.
predicates.quasi_judicial_assessment: The tax authority determines the assessment in a quasi-judicial capacity.
predicates.appellate_review: The assessment choice can be reviewed on appeal by higher tax authorities.
predicates.public_revenue_duty: The tax authority is responsible for collecting revenue lawfully due and preventing tax evasion or escape.
predicates.evasion_risk: Assessing the association may risk evasion of tax or escape from tax liability.
predicates.double_taxation_risk: The assessment must avoid taxing the same income more than once.

issues.definition: When a tax assessment allows a choice between collective and individual assessment, the choice is not unconstitutional if it is guided by quasi-judicial assessment or appellate review, serves the public revenue duty, and addresses evasion or double-taxation risks.

issues.legal_issue: A firm, an individual, and a minor represented by a consenting guardian may form an association of persons for the purpose of producing income.
material_facts: The properties were used in a trading venture and managed as a single unit by a firm.
The firm and the property owners used a common selling agency, maintained common accounts, and did not separately determine the venture’s stock and expenditure.
The minor had a share in the income, and the tribunal inferred that the minor’s guardian assented to the management arrangement on the minor’s behalf.
The assessment years at issue involved the individual, the firm, and the minor in the income-producing arrangement.
issues.conclusion: The evidence supported the finding that the individual, the firm, and the minor formed an association of persons in the relevant years.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, read with section 2(9) of that Act and section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act, a firm is a person and may form an association of persons with an individual or group of individuals. The Act does not prevent a minor from being a member of such an association; a guardian’s implied consent may support the finding that the minor participated. An association requires persons to join in a common purpose or action directed at producing income, profits, or gains. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income-tax v. Laxmidas and Commissioner of Income-tax v. Indira Balkrishna.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment_of_income_venture and (firm_and_individuals_joined or firm_and_individual_joined) and common_income_purpose and (common_management or common_business_operations) and minor_participation_assented_to

predicates.income_tax_assessment_of_income_venture: The proceeding assesses income earned through a venture for income-tax purposes.
predicates.firm_and_individuals_joined: A firm and one or more individuals joined in the venture.
predicates.firm_and_individual_joined: A firm and an individual joined in the venture.
predicates.common_income_purpose: The participants joined for a common purpose of producing income, profits, or gains.
predicates.common_management: The participants’ property or venture was managed together as a common unit.
predicates.common_business_operations: The participants conducted material business operations together, such as using common accounts or a common selling agency.
predicates.minor_participation_assented_to: A minor had a role or interest in the venture, and the minor’s guardian assented to the participation on the minor’s behalf.

issues.definition: A firm and individuals form an assessable association when they join in an income-producing purpose and operate or manage the venture together, including where a minor’s participation is assented to by a guardian.

issues.legal_issue: A finding in an assessment for one year does not bind the decision-maker in an assessment for another year, although it may be evidentially relevant.
material_facts: The High Court found that no association existed in one assessment year.
The tribunal found that an association existed in later assessment years, when the participants and arrangement differed.
The later finding was supported by evidence concerning the changed ownership shares, management arrangement, and business operations.
issues.conclusion: The earlier finding did not bind the tribunal in deciding whether an association existed in the later assessment years; the earlier finding could be considered as evidence but was not conclusive.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of res judicata does not make a finding of fact or law in an income-tax assessment for one year binding in another year. Each assessment and its findings are conclusive for that year alone, though findings may be cogent evidence in a subsequent year. The Court also noted that the later income-producing association was different from the one considered for the earlier year.

predicates.annual_tax_assessment: The proceeding determines tax liability separately for a particular assessment year.
predicates.prior_year_finding: A court or tribunal made a finding about a fact or legal issue in an earlier assessment year.
predicates.subsequent_year_assessment: A court or tribunal must determine the corresponding fact or legal issue for a later assessment year.

issues.definition: In a later annual tax assessment, a finding from an earlier assessment is not binding, though it may be considered as evidence.

issues.legal_issue: An assessment of an association may proceed without a prior adjudication declaring a person to be its principal officer if that person is duly served with the prescribed notice and the assessment order finds that the person is the principal officer.
material_facts: A person connected with the association was served with notice of the intention to treat him as its principal officer and received the assessment notices in that capacity.
The assessment order identified that person as the association’s principal officer.
The association could challenge that finding in appeals from the assessment.
issues.conclusion: A prior formal adjudication of the person’s status as principal officer was not required before assessment proceedings began, and the assessment order’s finding was sufficient compliance.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(12), 22(2), 34, and 63(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, a notice could be served on a person connected with an association whom the authority intended to treat as its principal officer. If the person was duly served in the prescribed manner, the authority could determine that status in the assessment order, subject to appeal; the order was not void merely because no prior declaration had been made. The Court applied the analogous principle in Commissioner of Income-tax, Punjab & N.W.F.P. v. Nawal Kishore Kharaiti Lal, concerning service on a person treated as an agent of a non-resident.

predicates.income_tax_assessment_of_association: The proceeding assesses the income of an association for tax purposes.
predicates.connected_person_received_prescribed_not: A person connected with the association received notice, served in the prescribed manner, that the authority intended to treat that person as its principal officer.
predicates.assessment_order_identifies_principal_of: The assessment order finds that the person served is the association’s principal officer.
predicates.appeal_available: The association can challenge the principal-officer finding in an appeal against the assessment.

issues.definition: An association’s assessment may proceed without an earlier formal declaration of principal-officer status when a connected person received the prescribed notice, the assessment order makes the finding, and an appeal is available.
